fetched_contents.text: Home • Patient Resources • Blog Eye Emergencies: When to Go to the ER vs Urgent Care Your vision is irreplaceable. When something goes wrong with your eyes, knowing where to seek help and how quickly can make the difference between preserving your sight and facing permanent vision loss. Not every eye problem requires a trip to the emergency room, but some absolutely do. Research shows that nearly half of emergency room visits for eye issues could be better handled at an urgent care facility or ophthalmology office. At the same time, certain eye emergencies can cause irreversible damage within minutes to hours if not treated immediately. This guide helps you understand which eye problems demand immediate ER care, which can wait for urgent care or same-day appointments, and what steps to take while getting help. As your San Diego eye care team at Clearview, we want you equipped to make the right call when every minute counts. ---------------------------------------- Understanding Eye Emergencies: What Makes Them Different? An eye emergency is any sudden or severe condition that threatens your vision or requires immediate medical action to prevent permanent damage. Research from emergency departments shows that only about 13% of patients presenting with eye complaints actually have true emergencies, while 60% have relative emergencies and 27% have non-urgent conditions. ---------------------------------------- True Eye Emergencies (Get Help Within Minutes to Hours) These situations demand immediate attention because delayed treatment can cause permanent vision loss: * Chemical burns or splashes in the eye * Penetrating eye injuries or trauma * Sudden, complete vision loss * Retinal detachment * Acute angle-closure glaucoma * Severe eye trauma with visible damage or bleeding * Objects embedded or impaled in the eye ---------------------------------------- Relative Eye Emergencies (Need Same-Day Care) These need prompt evaluation but aren't immediately sight-threatening: * Foreign objects like metal shavings or wood splinters * Corneal scratches (abrasions) * Eye infections with pain or discharge * New flashing lights or sudden increase in floaters * Sudden double vision * Temporary vision loss (even if it comes back) ---------------------------------------- Why Time Matters So Much Unlike other medical emergencies where you might have hours or days, some eye conditions can cause irreversible vision loss within 60 to 90 minutes if left untreated. ---

## 3. Stroke versus non-stroke sudden vision loss

### Stroke-related causes and symptoms
Stroke-related vision loss is centered on **central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO)**, often called an **eye stroke**, and other vascular events that can affect the visual system [N6-F2][N6-R5]. The branch reports also note that sudden vision loss can be a sign of a stroke [N6-R3], and that people with sudden vision loss caused by retinal artery occlusion or eye stroke should be treated with the same urgency as those with brain stroke [N6-R4].

Specific stroke-related symptoms include:
- **Vision loss in one eye**
- **Field cut** or **partial loss of vision**
- **Blurred vision**
- **Double vision**
- **Loss of visual field**
- **Other stroke symptoms**, such as weakness, speech issues, headache, or altered mental status [N6-R1][N6-R3][N7-R5][N7-R2]

The branch reports emphasize that the key distinction is whether the vision loss fits a vascular pattern and whether there are associated neurological signs [N6-F2][N6-R3][N5-R3]. Stroke-related vision loss is often **abrupt and unilateral**, and it can be associated with other stroke symptoms. However, the evidence also says that sudden vision changes may also be caused by other conditions, so a single symptom alone is not enough to diagnose a stroke [N6-R3].

In short, if you have sudden vision loss in one eye **without pain**, and especially if you have other neurological symptoms, **stroke is a serious possibility** [N6-R3][N6-R4]. The evidence supports treating such cases with the same urgency as brain stroke [N6-R4].

### What the patient should know about urgency and downstream risk
The branch reports are very clear about urgency and downstream risk:
- Stroke affecting the eye requires **immediate treatment** and can signal **future vascular events** [N6-F2]
- Early treatment generally leads to the best outcomes for an eye stroke [N6-F2]
- Some eye emergencies can cause irreversible damage within minutes to hours, so time matters a lot [N5-F3]
- Temporary vision loss can signal an impending stroke or other serious condition [N5-F3]

So the patient should not wait to see if the vision loss resolves. The evidence says that even if vision improves on its own, you still need emergency evaluation [N5-F3].

---

## 4. What the patient should do next: clinical evaluation and specialist care pathway

### What an ophthalmologist will check
The branch reports indicate that the clinical evaluation should begin with **prompt specialist involvement** because sudden vision loss is treated as an emergency [N1-F1][N5-F3]. The ophthalmologist will typically check:
- The **fundus** to assess the retina and optic nerve
- The **visual field**
- Other signs of retinal or optic nerve involvement [N5-F3][N5-R2]

The evidence also says that same-day care is crucial for determining the underlying cause [N5-F3]. The Cleveland Clinic source says that sudden vision loss can often improve with quick medical attention [N1-F1].

### When to see a neurologist or other specialist
If the provider suspects a neurological cause or stroke-related involvement, a **neurologist** may be involved. The evidence says that sudden vision loss can be a sign of a stroke or eye stroke, and that people with sudden vision loss caused by retinal artery occlusion or eye stroke should be treated with the same urgency as those with brain stroke [N6-R4][N6-F2]. Stroke Canada also notes that blurred vision or partial/complete vision loss may be signs of a stroke [N6-R3]. Because stroke can affect vision in one eye and can have serious downstream vascular risk, the provider may consider a neurology referral if the clinical picture suggests a vascular event [N6-F2][N6-R3].

### Tests that may be needed
The branch reports support several tests depending on the suspected cause:
- **Fundoscopy** to examine the retina and optic nerve [N5-F3][N5-R2]
- **Visual field testing** because sudden vision loss is a red flag that may be associated with field changes [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-F4]

---

## 5. What the patient should not do

- Do **not** assume that no pain means it is not urgent [N1-F1][N5-R3]
- Do **not** wait to see if vision improves on its own [N5-F3]
- Do **not** delay seeking care because the loss is painless [N1-F1][N5-R2]
- Do **not** self-diagnose or assume the loss is minor [N5-F3]
- Do **not** try to determine the cause on your own [N5-F3]

---

## Bottom line

If you suddenly lose vision in your left eye **without pain**, the best and safest answer is:

> **Go to the emergency room immediately.**

The evidence supports treating sudden vision loss in one eye as a **medical emergency**, whether it is painful or not [N1-F1][N5-F3]. 1. **Call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room immediately.**
2. **Note the exact nature of the vision loss and any associated symptoms.**
3. **Do not delay treatment.**

The patient should **describe the loss in detail** for the doctor. The branch reports emphasize that the timeline, pattern, and severity matter. You should note:
